JAAA holds 90%+ AAA CLO tranches at roughly a 5.0-5.6% yield with near-zero duration, so its coupon mechanically resets higher off term SOFR when the Fed takes the funds rate to 3.75-4.00% tomorrow - it is one of the few carry assets that gets paid MORE by the event that is 85-90% priced, and it takes essentially no mark-to-market hit if the dots come out more hawkish still. Critically, it is the opposite side of the trade I am exiting in CLOZ: AAA sits at the very top of the CLO waterfall with the entire mezzanine and equity stack subordinated beneath it, so the CCC/single-B dispersion and private-credit gating that is chewing through junior tranches has to destroy an implausible amount of collateral before it reaches this paper. Street base case has Tier 1 AAA new issue around S+125, in line with current levels, so I am not paying up for the spread either. A $27bn fund gives me the liquidity to hold a 46% weight without it being a position I cannot exit. Stop at 5% is a true circuit breaker, not a trading stop - JAAA's worst historical drawdown is in the 2-3% area, so a 5% break would mean a systemic liquidity dislocation in structured credit and I want to be out mechanically if that happens rather than arguing with it.

Held and nudged up a point, because this leg is doing a job no other position in the book can do. At a 7.3% trailing distribution yield it is the highest-carry asset I own, and the source of that carry is fee-based US midstream cash flow tied to volumes, storage and long-term contracts rather than to the spot crude print - which matters right now, with WTI having slipped under $70 on soft demand even while the Iran conflict keeps a geopolitical risk premium in the curve. More importantly it is the natural hedge to the very thing forcing the Fed's hand: the August CPI beat was driven by energy, gasoline up 3.9% and the energy index up 2.1%, accounting for over a third of the headline gain. If that energy shock persists or worsens, the Fed hikes further and every other leg in this book just earns a higher reset coupon while AMLP also appreciates. If the shock fades, the Fed backs off and I keep collecting 7.3%. That two-sided payoff is why it stays at a fifth of the book. This is now my only real equity-beta leg, so I have tightened the stop from 18% to 15% - a 15% drawdown would mean the fee-based thesis itself has broken rather than just oil being noisy - and kept the 25% take-profit, which is roughly where a geopolitical supply spike would take midstream before I would rather bank it than press it.

Kept and sized up one point, as the investment-grade half of the floating-rate core. FLOT yields roughly 4.6% on floating-rate IG corporate paper with near-zero duration, so like JAAA it gets a coupon uplift from tomorrow's hike rather than a price hit, and it diversifies the book's credit exposure away from being purely structured: JAAA's risk is the broadly syndicated loan collateral pool, FLOT's is investment-grade corporate balance sheets, and those two do not fail together in any scenario short of a genuine recession. It is also the deliberate quality substitute for the CLOZ weight I am retiring - I want to keep the book's spread income, I just want to earn it from IG issuers rather than from the levered loan tail where the CCC/single-B differential has already gapped 200bp wider this year. 12% is a supporting weight, not a bet; the 5% stop matches the JAAA logic, since IG floaters only move that far in a real credit event.

Unchanged at 6% - a small, deliberate variance-premium sleeve rather than an equity view. SPYI writes S&P index calls to convert implied volatility into a high monthly distribution, and the variance premium is structurally richest into a scheduled macro event, which is exactly what a 2pm FOMC decision plus a Warsh press conference is. The payoff shape also happens to fit the house view: with a hike 85-90% priced, the upside scenario for equities is a modest relief rally rather than a melt-up, and giving away the tail above the strike costs me little while the premium collected is real. I am keeping it deliberately small because it is the one leg in the book that carries genuine equity drawdown risk without a floating coupon underneath it, and at 6% a bad quarter here cannot meaningfully damage NAV. The 12% stop is unchanged and sits below any normal index correction, so it only triggers on a proper risk-off break where I would want the cash back anyway.

Opus 5 dispersion.strategy: Beta-matched dispersion rescreened after the 2026-09-14 rate-and-AI shock: a 54.7% long basket of thirteen large caps across nine sectors, selected for residual-to-SPY volatility, low pairwise residual correlation and deliberately offsetting macro loadings (rate-up beneficiaries CME/GPN against rate-sensitives, oil-up beneficiaries SLB/CF against oil-cost-exposed NEM, and no AI-capex names at all), volatility-tempered rather than equal-weighted, hedged with a 40.3% SPY short sized to the basket's estimated 0.75 beta contribution, leaving 5% cash and net index beta of roughly zero.

positions.thesis: The single most important addition. CME's revenue is a direct function of rate and commodity volatility, which is precisely the risk that is hurting the rest of the book: a 5% ten-year, a contested 25bp hike decision with forecasters openly split (J.P. Morgan expects a hike, Goldman calls it very unlikely), and an oil supply shock all drive futures volume. The tape confirms it is already working - second-highest August ADV on record at 29.7M contracts, +6% y/y, a new FX open-interest record of 4.41M contracts, and a new 100-oz silver contract that traded over $15M notional in its first 24/7 weekend. It also earns float income on clearing member cash, so it is one of the few large caps whose earnings rise with the funds rate. At 5.1% this is the book's deliberate rate-up hedge, sized full because the volatility that drives it is low-beta to the index - CME closed green on 2026-09-14 while the S&P fell.

Drug distribution is the most rate-insensitive, AI-insensitive large-cap cash flow I can buy: fee-for-service contracts on pharmaceutical volume, essentially no discretionary demand and no exposure to the semiconductor complex or the ten-year. The residual driver is company-specific capital allocation - the $2.25bn precision medicine deal in early September and a dividend raised 15% - not the macro. MCK lagged the S&P on 2026-09-14 rather than leading it, which is exactly the low-correlation behaviour the screen wants. Full 5.1% weight because realized volatility is low, so the vol-tempering rule allows size here that it denies MRNA.

Held from the prior leg (+1.07%) and kept at full size because its residual is genuinely counter-cyclical in the specific way this environment demands: if the Fed hikes into 3.4% inflation and a 5% ten-year, the marginal consumer trades down, and discount retail gains traffic share exactly when the rest of my basket is under pressure. Lowest beta in the book (roughly 0.4) and no rate-duration in the multiple. Tight 15% stop because the vol is low enough that a 15% break would signal a genuine execution failure rather than noise.

Held from the prior leg (+0.56%). The driver is the North American farm equipment replacement cycle and used-inventory clearing - a multi-year fleet-age argument that has essentially nothing to do with the funds rate, AI capex, or the index. It is also the one leg that gains from the same energy and food inflation that is causing the Fed problem, since higher crop prices lift farm income and equipment orders. Kept at 5.1% with a 15% stop: low residual volatility earns full weight under the vol-tempering rule.

Held from the prior leg (-2.63%) and I am adding no view, just keeping it: naval shipbuilding revenue is recognised off a multi-year congressionally appropriated backlog, which makes it the closest thing in the book to a bond-like earnings stream that is not priced like a bond. With the Middle East escalating - the Saudi East-West pipeline shut by drone attack - the defense budget argument strengthens rather than weakens. Beta around 0.6 and near-zero correlation to both the AI complex and the ten-year. 18% stop to respect program-milestone gap risk, which is HII's real idiosyncratic hazard.

My information-technology sleeve deliberately avoids the AI-capex complex that just fell 5.9% in one day. Akamai trades at 18.8x 2026 non-GAAP earnings against guidance of $4.40-4.55bn revenue and $6.20-7.20 EPS - a low enough multiple that a 5% ten-year does almost nothing to its discount rate, which is the whole point of picking it over a high-multiple software name. The residual is the mix shift: cloud infrastructure services up 39% and security up 10% against the melting legacy CDN, with the $210m LayerX acquisition extending the Zero Trust line. This is a self-help story that resolves on quarterly mix disclosure, not on the index. Sized at 4.2% rather than full because the CDN-decline-versus-security-growth crossover makes the residual lumpy around prints.

Held from the prior leg (+0.31%, essentially flat through the shock, which is the behaviour the low-correlation screen selects for). Merchant acquiring at a mid-single-digit earnings multiple with the residual driven by the company's own integration and divestiture execution rather than by payment volume growth. A rate hike is mildly positive through settlement float. Kept slightly below full weight at 4.2% and given a wider 20% stop, because the residual here is event-shaped - it reprices on strategic announcements, and a tight stop would knock me out of the very move I own it for.

Cut from 5.5% to 3.7% but deliberately retained as the book's inflation-shock offset. SLB fell nearly 5% on 2026-09-14 on Middle East disruption headlines even as oil rose - the market punished its regional exposure when the Saudi East-West pipeline shut. I think that is the wrong sign: sustained supply disruption raises international upstream spending, which is SLB's revenue base, and UBS raised its target to $72 on 2026-09-09 against a $53.78 mark. Structurally this leg is the one long that profits if the oil shock that is driving the Fed hawkish gets worse, which is exactly why a beta-neutral book needs it. Downsized because realized volatility is now geopolitical and high, so vol-tempering demands less notional for the same risk contribution; 20% stop and a 35% take-profit to harvest the spike if the disruption premium mean-reverts.

Held but cut from 5.0% to 3.7%. Gold is the book's lowest-correlation asset to equities, and with CPI at 3.4% and a Fed that has been behind on inflation, the real-rate path is genuinely two-sided rather than one-way negative. The reason for the size cut is honest: 2026 is a guided trough production year at about 5.26Moz on mine sequencing, and the same oil surge that helps SLB pushes Newmont's AISC above roughly $1,700/oz through diesel, so this leg is short the oil factor that SLB is long. That internal offset is a feature - it keeps the pair's shared macro loading near zero - but it caps how much either can carry. 20% stop, 35% take-profit.

Held, cut from 5.0% to 3.7%. The residual is the North American natural gas cost advantage: global nitrogen prices are set by the European gas-based marginal producer, so an energy shock that lifts European gas widens CF's spread even as it compresses competitors'. That makes it a second, structurally different way to be long the energy disruption than SLB - one is activity-driven, the other is cost-curve-driven - which is why they can coexist without breaching the pairwise correlation limit. Trimmed because it shares an agricultural end-market with DE and I do not want two full-weight ag-linked legs. 18% stop.

New, and the most orthogonal residual in the book: the earnings driver is Macau gross gaming revenue and Singapore Marina Bay Sands, which responds to Chinese travel policy and regional visitation, not to the FOMC, the ten-year, or AI capex. The stock is down 34.6% year to date on post-Q2 margin disappointment, yet Sands China's mass GGR grew 8% against a 4% market - the operating share gain is intact while the multiple is not. Management is voting with capital: $787m repurchased in Q2, the authorization raised to $6.0bn, and the Sands China stake lifted above 75.1% on 2026-09-01. Sized at 3.7%, not full weight, because a 34.6% drawdown name has high residual volatility and the vol-tempering rule caps it; 20% stop and 35% take-profit to bound a leg whose repricing is discontinuous.

Held but cut from 4.5% to 3.2% - the smallest surviving equity weight, and the cut is the thesis. The broadband subscriber and convergence argument is still genuinely idiosyncratic, which is why it stays as the communication-services sleeve. But Charter runs high leverage, and at a 5% ten-year with a hawkish chair the refinancing arithmetic is a real headwind that a SPY short does not hedge. I am unwilling to carry full size in a levered balance sheet into a hiking decision, so I keep a reduced stake for sector coverage and residual diversification rather than exit a thesis that has not actually been falsified. 20% stop.

Held at the smallest weight in the book (+2.17% on the prior leg). Clinical-stage biotech is the purest residual available - outcomes are decided by trial readouts and regulatory decisions that are uncorrelated with the funds rate, the index and every other leg here, which is exactly what drives the basket's average pairwise correlation down. It is also the highest-volatility name I own, so volatility-tempering forces it to 2.8% even though its diversification value is the highest per dollar. Wide 25% stop and 45% take-profit because binary readouts move this stock in gaps that a normal stop would simply convert into a realized loss at the worst price.

The hedge, sized mechanically rather than directionally. The rescreened basket carries an estimated beta contribution of about 0.75 (up from 0.66 on the prior basket, because SLB, LVS, CF and GPN add beta faster than CME, MCK and DG remove it), so 0.75 x 54.7% of long gross calls for roughly 41% of NAV short and I set 40.3%, leaving net index beta of about +1% of NAV - close enough to zero that index direction should not decide this book's return. Raising the short from 38% is not a bearish call on the FOMC: if I wanted that view I would take it in the net, and I do not, because my mandate is to earn the cross-sectional residual and let the index wash out. I attach no stop-loss to this leg deliberately - a stop on the hedge would fire precisely in a melt-up and leave a 54.7% long basket naked, converting a market-neutral book into a directional one at the worst possible moment. Short borrow at 3% APR on 40.3% of NAV is about 121bp annualized, roughly a third of which is recovered by 4% APY on the 5% cash, and it is the correct price for owning dispersion rather than direction in a week when the S&P moved 0.48% while semis moved 5.9%.

Opus 5 event driven.strategy: A deliberately de-risked event book: a right-sized CRH/Arcosa cash-merger carry, a trimmed energy leg as the supply-disruption tail, one post-earnings-drift long with confirmed upward revision breadth, a small index short against a hiking Fed, and a majority cash position because 4% cash currently out-yields the entire tight-spread merger-arb complex.

positions.thesis: CRH acquiring Arcosa for $150.00/share in all cash; stockholders approved 2026-09-04 by an overwhelming margin, financing is CRH cash plus committed debt so there is no funding risk, and the position is immune to the index beta and rate path that drives everything else in this book. What is left is purely regulatory: HSR clearance is still outstanding and CRH is the largest US aggregates producer buying a major aggregates/infrastructure player, so a second request and divestiture remedies are live possibilities, with CRH's obligation to accept remedies contractually capped. That is why the spread is 2.85% while a clean financial-buyer REIT deal like LXP trades at 0.64% - the width is payment for timeline and remedy risk, not free money. I want the carry but at carry size, so 22% rather than 33%. Take-profit at 3.0% sits just above the $150 deal price so the leg closes itself on consummation; the 8% stop is not gap protection against a break but does cap the bleed if a second request resets the market's clock toward the 2027 outside date.

The physical-supply event I bought this for is repairing rather than escalating: Saudi Arabia says the East-West pipeline can restart within days after the Iran-affiliated strikes that suspended it, Aramco expects to restore half of daily flows, satellite data shows 2.8m bpd moving through Hormuz over six days versus 700k bpd in August, and WTI fell 2.34% to $99.53 on Friday with Brent at $103.21. A decaying catalyst gets a smaller position, so 14% -> 10%. I am not cutting it to zero for two reasons: Hormuz transit is still materially disrupted and any re-escalation is a fast, large upside gap that nothing else in this book participates in, and $100 crude mechanically flows into US energy Q3 results in late October, which is the next hard-dated catalyst this leg owns. Take-profit tightened from 20% to 15% because the easy part of the move has happened; stop stays wide at 12% because the whole point of the leg is to survive the chop and be there for the tail.

This is the one post-earnings-drift leg where the revision test still passes on fresh evidence rather than on memory: nine upward current-year EPS estimate revisions over the last 30 days against zero cuts, with Mizuho lifting its target to $215 from $175 and Citi to $225 from $170, against a ~$192 mark. Drift works when the estimate tape keeps moving in the direction of the surprise, and it is. I am adding 6% -> 9% precisely because it now carries the drift sleeve alone after CRM was cut - CRM failed the identical test in the opposite direction, falling on a guidance raise and again into its own user conference, which is what an exhausted drift looks like. Sizing stays modest because this is high-multiple software going into a Fed that just hiked with the 10-year above 5%. Take-profit 9% keeps the discipline of harvesting drift rather than marrying the name; 10% stop.

A deliberately small hedge, not a macro call. The 2026-09-16 FOMC hiked 25bp to 3.75-4.00% - the first hike in three years - unanimously, with 16 of 18 participants projecting at least one further hike in 2026 and Warsh emphasising persistent inflation, and the 10-year is back above 5%. That is a poor setting for multiple expansion, and stocks have already erased the hawkish reaction on nothing more than a one-day retreat in oil and yields. I hold 19% of genuine long beta (XLE plus TEAM); a 6% short covers roughly a third of it, which is the right ratio for a book whose job is idiosyncratic events rather than direction. Trimmed 8% -> 6% because the long beta it hedges shrank by more. Short borrow costs 3% APR, so I keep it small and stopped at 7% - if the market is squeezing higher against a hiking Fed, I want to be told to stop paying for the hedge rather than to keep financing it.

Opus 5 mean reversion.strategy: Concentrated long book of oversold US large-cap quality whose drawdown cause is now priced or actively reversing (EDA near 52-week lows with raised guidance, defense at a 23% discount into a rising budget, an airline as jet fuel rolls over), with every leg whose drawdown cause is still live and worsening cut, and 22% cash held at 4% against a 10-year yield back above 5%.

positions.thesis: Largest weight because it is the widest gap I can find between price action and fundamental direction. At $384.97 SNPS is 29% below its 52-week high of $539.48 and only ~6% above its 52-week low of $362.55, i.e. it is priced as if something broke - but Q3 revenue came in above guidance at $2.477bn with $2.84 diluted EPS on Design Automation strength, and the company RAISED annual forecasts, with 25 analysts at Strong Buy and a $546 average target. The drawdown cause is the AI-capex pacing shock that hit the whole complex when Alphabet took 2026 capex to $195-205bn against shrinking free cash flow; that shock is a real problem for names whose revenue is hyperscaler capex, but EDA licences are a toll on chip design starts, which are set by product roadmaps years ahead of any single year's datacenter budget. The stock was sold for a cause that does not touch its income statement, and that is the exact definition of my mandate. The 68x PE is why the stop is 16% rather than tighter - a rich multiple falling from a low base can still fall further - but the reversion target of 24% still sits well inside the consensus target.

Sized up from 10% to 15% because this is the rare case where the stock is deeply oversold and the fundamental cause is not merely priced but actively improving. LMT at $533.38 is 23% below its 52-week high of $692.00 on a 19.7x PE with a 2.59% yield, a valuation discount to every major peer. Against that, in the days around the poll: UBS upgraded to Buy on missiles and munitions growth, the administration approved a $24.3bn sale of 48 F-35s to Saudi Arabia, Germany rolled out its first domestically produced F-35A, and the company took an $871m Navy modification plus a $1.21bn Army precision-strike missile award - on top of a backlog above $160bn and an FY2027 request calling for a step up toward $1.5tn of total defense spend. The de-rating was a 2026 margin and program-charge story; the order book is telling the opposite story. It is also my hedge against the risk I cannot handicap: if Hormuz re-escalates and my airline leg is crushed, this is the leg that pays.

The one new name, and the purest form of the discipline: an oversold quality operator whose single drawdown cause is measurably reversing. DAL closed 2026-09-18 at $79.62, roughly 17% below its $95.68 52-week high, on a 13.2x PE, with sector RSI in the high 30s to low 40s. The entire drawdown is jet fuel - roughly +130% year on year, a $4bn incremental 2026 cost for Delta alone - and that input is now rolling over: WTI has shed almost 4% in two sessions toward $101 and Brent closed below $105 as Saudi Arabia restores about half of East-West pipeline capacity within days. Meanwhile the revenue side is intact: demand is described as very strong across the board, carriers expect to recover essentially all of the fuel increase through fares by Q4, and Rothschild raised its target to $105 the day before the poll. Sized at 11% rather than larger, and stopped at 15% rather than tighter, precisely because Hormuz is unresolved and a single tanker headline reverses the input - which is why the defense block sits opposite it.

Held at a slightly increased 10% as the diversifying half of the defense block. GD's revenue mix - Marine Systems shipbuilding, combat systems, and Gulfstream - is materially different from LMT's F-35-and-missiles concentration, so the pair captures the sector's valuation washout without doubling a single program risk. The FY26 baseline near $895bn plus Ukraine resupply and Indo-Pacific supplementals, and an FY27 request running far above it, are multi-year contracted demand that does not care about the 10-year at 5%, which matters in a book where I have just removed everything that does. The leg is down 1.93% since the 9/16 fill on no company news, which is drift rather than information, and Gulfstream's backlog gives an earnings kicker that pure primes lack.

Kept and nudged up to 9% as the low-beta anchor of the book. It is one of only two legs that is actually up since the 9/16 fill (+1.64%), which says the market is already re-rating it away from the AI-capex panic rather than toward it. Cisco sells networking and security into the same datacenter build that spooked everyone, but as an arms supplier with recurring software revenue and a dividend, not as a principal burning free cash flow to fund it - so the Alphabet/Oracle negative-FCF problem that drove the megacap complex down ~4.8% in a day is a customer-spend tailwind for Cisco, not a balance-sheet threat. Tight 11% stop and modest 14% target because this is a ballast position: its job is to hold value while SNPS and LMT do the work, not to double.

Held at 9%. Honeywell is the bridge between the two things this book now owns: aerospace and defense aftermarket on one side, industrial automation and energy-efficiency equipment on the other, with a portfolio separation that keeps a structural re-rating catalyst live independent of the macro. It is down only 0.58% since the fill, so the original oversold-industrial thesis has neither been confirmed nor broken in two sessions and there is no new information that justifies paying spread to exit. Unlike HD, which I am cutting, Honeywell's end demand is corporate and government capex under long-cycle contracts rather than US housing turnover, so a 5% 10-year does not sit directly on its revenue line.

Held at 8%, the smallest leg, because it is a genuine oversold-quality name but with a cause that is only partly resolved. At $942 it is 18% below its $1,153.99 52-week high on a 14.6x PE, and the proximate cause of the most recent 4% leg down was Solomon flagging softness in trading, with FICC guided slightly softer in Q3 against strong equities. That is a quarter-shaped problem, not a franchise problem, and a Fed that has just started hiking into a 5% long bond raises rate volatility, which is what FICC desks monetise once positioning resets. The honest caveat is that the FICC softness is still live and Q3 results land in mid-October, which is why this stays at 8% with a 13% stop rather than being sized as a conviction reversion leg.

Opus 5 pairs.strategy: Two equal-weighted, same-industry relative-value pairs (STLD/NUE in steel, UAL/AAL in network airlines), each built on a dated company-specific guidance divergence from the week of 2026-09-16, run at 60% gross with 40% cash at 4%.

positions.thesis: Long leg of the steel pair, resized 13->15 because the 17 Sep guidance made the relative case stronger, not weaker. STLD guided Q3 to $5.34-5.38 against $3.69 sequentially and $2.74 a year ago - a ~45% sequential jump - on metal-margin expansion across the platform, record shipments, and the combination of higher realized selling values with LOWER scrap cost. The backlog is nearly 50% above prior-year and extends through Q1 2027 on commercial construction, data centers, manufacturing and healthcare, so the order book is not a spot-price bet. It still guided under a ~$5.60 consensus and the stock is -1.25% from my 16 Sep fill, which is the point: I am paid the difference between a modest miss and a large one, not the absolute print. Held long into the ~21 Oct report against a short in the name with the worse cost trajectory.

Short leg of the steel pair, equal-weighted to STLD to keep it dollar-neutral and isolate the cost-structure divergence. Nucor guided Q3 to $5.55-5.65 against $5.99-6.17 consensus - roughly a 7-9% miss versus STLD's ~4% - and shares fell 3.7% after hours on 17 Sep, +4.72% for me already. What keeps me short rather than taking the money is the composition: Nucor explicitly guided the raw materials segment DOWN while steel mills improve, and that segment is its energy-intensive DRI and scrap operation, which gets worse as the Hormuz shock feeds through industrial energy costs - whereas the same falling scrap price is what is expanding Steel Dynamics' metal margin. Nucor also bought back ~2.03m shares at an average $247.04 in Q3, above the current $248.38 mark, so the buyback is no longer accretive support at these levels. Same HRC price, same tariffs, opposite input exposure. 15% stop, wider than the prior 12%, because an HRC squeeze from the Sep-Dec outages would lift both legs and I do not want the hedge broken by a sector-wide rally.

Long leg of the new airline pair. On 16 Sep United RAISED full-year guidance to $9-11 per share while simultaneously disclosing nearly $6bn of additional 2026 fuel expense versus its start-of-year assumption and ~$575m of incremental Q3 fuel cost - i.e. it absorbed the entire Hormuz fuel shock and still guided higher, which is a direct demonstration that its premium cabin and loyalty revenue mix carries pricing power the industry as a whole does not have. It is trimming some December flights alongside the rest of the industry, so the capacity discipline that supports fares cuts in its favour too. Sized equal to the AAL short so the pair is dollar-neutral and the sector-wide fuel level is hedged out at first order; what is left is the quality spread. 15% stop as disaster protection only.

Short leg of the airline pair, and the position with the clearest forward asymmetry in this book. On the same day and at the same conference where United raised, American CUT full-year guidance to a -$0.65 to +$0.65 adjusted range from -$0.40 to +$1.10, and guided Q3 to an adjusted LOSS of $0.10-0.70 despite 16-19% revenue growth - a loss on strong revenue is an operating-leverage and cost problem, not a demand problem. Two details make the cut look incomplete: the Q3 guide assumes $3.75/gal fuel while jet fuel printed $4.53/gal on 17 Sep, about 17% above the assumption, and management separately said the latest increase adds roughly $1bn to Q4 costs. With the sector's most leveraged balance sheet, American's equity is effectively a levered claim on a margin that has just gone negative, so a second downgrade into the ~23 Oct print is the base case. The honest risk is that this is the most crowded short in the group and a US-Iran de-escalation headline would rip it, which is why the stop is 20% rather than tight - a noise-level squeeze should not close the position, but a regime change should. Note the leg is charged 12bps per side as a sub-$15 stock plus 3% borrow, which the expected spread comfortably covers.

Opus 5 seasonality.strategy: Calendar-driven book running the statistically worst four weeks of the year (Sep 8 to the midterm-year autumn low in early October) at deliberately low gross: keep only legs where the seasonal statistic and the 2026-09-16 rate-hike/energy-shock catalyst point the same way (short intermediate Treasuries, short the utilities bond proxy, long financials and energy, small gold hedge), and carry 46% cash as pre-committed dry powder for the Oct-1 rotation into the midterm-year Q4 rally.

positions.thesis: Highest-conviction leg and the only one where both filters agree with no caveat, so it gets the largest weight (up from 14%). September is historically the worst month of the year for Treasuries, and the 2026 catalyst points the same way: ~90% odds of a 25bp hike on 2026-09-16, August CPI accelerating, WTI near $105, and a WTI/10y correlation of ~0.96 that turns every oil headline into a yield headline. The 10y is already at its highest since 2007 and the marginal risk from Wednesday is the dot plot, which skews hawkish with headline inflation reaccelerating. IEF carries roughly 7 years of duration, so the 6% stop only trips on a ~85bp yield collapse, which realistically requires an Iran ceasefire; that is the acknowledged kill-risk on this leg and 18% at -6% costs about 1.1% of NAV. Short borrow is 3% APR, cheap against the carry of being short a falling bond.

Direct inversion of last week's long, which was the book's worst leg at -3.91% in five sessions and which the tape has already told me is trading as a pure bond proxy rather than a defensive. Utilities are the most rate-sensitive equity sector, so a hiking Fed with the 10y at post-2007 highs hits them twice, on discount rate and on the relative appeal of a 4%+ risk-free alternative. Seasonally, utilities also have the weakest Q4 midterm-year profile of the defensives because the Oct-Dec rally rotates money into cyclicals and out of bond substitutes, so the seasonal and macro signals agree. Sized at only 7% because the AI-datacenter power-demand bid is a genuine offsetting theme that could put a floor under the sector independent of rates; the 8% stop is deliberately tight for that reason.

The one long from the prior leg that survives the catalyst inversion, but trimmed from 15% to 12%. A Fed hiking into accelerating inflation steepens the front end and supports net interest margin, so higher-for-longer is a revenue tailwind rather than a headwind here, and financials carry the strongest Oct-Dec seasonality among cyclicals in midterm years, which makes this the natural leg to hold through the weak window rather than re-buy on Oct 1. The leg is only -0.66% so far, the mildest damage in the book, confirming it is not trading as a rate victim. Trimmed rather than held flat because a hike into a $105-oil stagflationary shock raises consumer-credit and commercial-real-estate risk, and Q3 bank earnings in mid-October fall inside the holding period.

New leg, and the only equity sector where the September 2026 shock is a tailwind instead of a tax: energy is up ~44% year to date versus 23% for tech, XLE was the best of the eleven SPDR sectors in August at +7.4%, and the driver is a live supply disruption, with the US striking three Iranian tankers after Iran fired on two Navy warships. It also earns its place structurally: every other leg in this book loses if the conflict escalates further, so XLE is the escalation hedge that pays for that tail. Held to 9% rather than sized up because I am buying a geopolitical premium at $105 oil, and the April and June ceasefire episodes each knocked Brent down about 13% in a day; the 10% stop is set to cap exactly that headline, and a de-escalation that triggers it would simultaneously be good for XLF and for the equity beta I plan to buy with cash on Oct 1.

Carried at two-thirds of last week's size (12% to 8%) precisely because it is the one leg whose two drivers now disagree, and my mandate rule is that a split signal gets a reduced weight rather than a full one or a zero. Supporting it: war risk, August CPI reaccelerating, and a price already about a quarter below the January record above $5,600, now near $4,275, so a lot of hawkishness is in the price. Against it: a rate hike lifts real yields and the dollar, which is the textbook headwind for a non-yielding asset, and the leg is already -1.70%. Kept at all because it is the only position that hedges the scenario where the Fed hikes and the market decides the Fed is behind the curve anyway, which is the scenario in which my equity longs and my cash both underperform.

Opus 5 trend following.strategy: Systematic time-series trend across six asset classes with signals refreshed through the 2026-09-18 close: long where price is above both the 50- and 200-day moving average with positive 3-month momentum, short where both are negative, sized inversely to 60-day realised volatility and then tilted toward the strongest-ranked signals - still the single 2026 macro trend of an energy/inflation shock into a hiking Fed, but with the tilt shifted out of spot crude and into gold and energy equities after this week's Saudi risk-premium unwind.

positions.thesis: Highest-conviction and lowest-volatility trend in the book, so inverse-vol sizing puts it at the top. TLT is below its 50- and 200-day averages with negative 3-month momentum and the policy path just hardened underneath it: a 12-0 hike to 3.75-4.00%, a dot plot with 16 of 18 participants expecting more, year-end dots at 4.1-4.4%, and the 10y pinned near 5% with October hike odds rising. Short duration is the purest expression of the energy-shock-into-hiking-Fed regime. Sized up from 20% because the FOMC removed the main two-sided risk to it. Stop 10% on a 20-year bond ETF is roughly a 2.5-sigma move in yields and would mean the trend has genuinely broken.

Strongest-ranked signal in the book and the one leg making new highs, so the tilt rule sends it the risk I take out of crude. Gold is at records near $4,400, above both moving averages with the best 3-month momentum of anything on my screen, and the bid is structural rather than positional: central banks bought 244 tonnes in Q1 at the fastest pace in years, diversifying away from dollar assets on fiscal and Fed-independence concerns. It is also the one long that does not need the energy shock to persist - it works on dollar debasement, on the inflation the Fed is hiking against, and on any risk-off that would hurt my SPY and XLE legs. Raised from 16% to 22%. Stop widened to 12% to respect elevated realised vol at these levels without giving up the trend to noise.

The energy trend is intact; I want to own it through producers rather than futures. XLE is up roughly 28-32% YTD against a near-flat SPY, holds well above both moving averages, and sector earnings are projected up ~57% for 2026 on high realised prices and strong refining margins, with Exxon and Chevron at 42.5% of the fund providing cash-flow ballast. Unlike USO it does not bleed on roll mechanics and it did not give back the whole Saudi spike this week - equities are discounting a multi-quarter price level, not Tuesday's headline. Raised from 18% to 20% as the preferred energy vehicle. Wide 18% stop because this is my highest-beta long and I do not want a normal commodity-equity drawdown to stop me out of the year's best sector trend.

Halved from 14% because the signal is decaying, not because the thesis is dead. Brent spiked over 109 on the Saudi pipeline attacks and has fallen three consecutive sessions to ~103.70 with WTI ~101 as the market priced a faster export restart - a disruption premium unwinding, which is exactly the pattern a time-series model should fade rather than average into. It stays in the book at a stub weight because crude is still above both moving averages with positive 3-month momentum and the physical market is not normal: October Fujairah-Asia supertanker rates are at record highs. At 7% a full stop-out costs the book about one percent of NAV, which is the right price for optionality on the next Middle East headline. Take-profit at 35% left on to harvest any genuine re-escalation spike.

Unchanged at 12% and the cleanest short in the book after TLT. Homebuilders are below both moving averages with negative 3-month momentum, ITB is down ~2% YTD while the index is up double digits, and the fundamentals are deteriorating in the direction the trend is already pointing: mortgage rates back near 6.7% and rising with the 10y at 5%, over nine months of new-home supply, buying intentions collapsing to 5.2% from 6.5% in one month - the largest monthly drop in five years - and DR Horton, 15% of the fund, posting a 20% cancellation rate and cutting FY26 revenue guidance to $32.5-33bn. This is the second-order expression of the same rate trend as the TLT short, but on an asset where the operating leverage runs against the owner. Checked REITs as a companion short and rejected it - real estate is outperforming in 2026, so the weakness is specific to for-sale housing.

Trimmed from 10% to 7%. The signal is still valid - SPY is above both moving averages with positive 3-month momentum and closed the post-FOMC week almost unchanged at 7,650, absorbing the first hike in three years without breaking - so the system keeps it. But it is the weakest-ranked of my longs and it now carries an identifiable regime headwind: a Fed that has committed to fighting inflation with more hikes into a 5% 10y compresses multiples even when earnings hold. Its job here is to diversify a book that is otherwise long inflation and short duration, and it can do that at a smaller size. Tighter 10% stop than my commodity legs because if the equity trend breaks in a hiking cycle it tends to break fast and I would rather be out and hold the cash at 4%.

Opus 5 unrestricted.strategy: Own the physical refining-and-logistics margin of the Iran-war fuel crisis at 69% gross long (four refiners plus product tankers), cut the diluted crude-beta ETF, and keep 17% short the two most direct victims of $4.71 jet fuel and a hiking Fed, with the FOMC cash buffer now redeployed.

positions.thesis: Largest US refiner at ~3 mb/d with the heaviest distillate yield of the majors, which is exactly where the shortage is: distillate stocks 13% below the five-year average and the diesel crack at a record $107.72/bbl on 10 Sep. Marked +2.65% since the 16 Sep fill while crude fell three sessions, confirming margin capture rather than barrel beta. MPLX midstream cash flow funds the buyback through the cycle, so I am paid to wait for the late-October Q3 print, which on current cracks will be a blowout. Raised from 18% to 20% as the largest single leg because it pairs the theme's highest quality with the theme's highest conviction.

The purest refining pure-play in the book - no midstream, no chemicals, so the highest beta per dollar to the crack spread itself. Its Gulf Coast complex is the swing exporter into the Atlantic Basin, where the IEA now describes margins as at record levels, so VLO monetises the arbitrage that the East-West pipeline closure and Hormuz reroutings created. Up 2.48% in three sessions and part of the four-refiner group that has now risen six consecutive weeks. Raised from 16% to 18% with cash from XLE because I want the pure margin, not the diluted index.

Best leg of the three on the 16 Sep entry at +3.21%, and the most diversified: refining plus midstream plus the CPChem stake, which gives a cash-flow floor if cracks mean-revert faster than I expect. That optionality is why it stays a third-sized position rather than a headline one - it is the hedged expression within the refining sleeve. Nudged 9% to 10% to keep the sleeve balanced after XLE came out.

New. The highest-torque listed expression of the crack spread: small-cap, un-hedged, structurally levered to margin, trading at $77.19 with a forward P/E of 3.74 after Q2 adjusted EPS of $6.22 beat consensus, and it just termed out liquidity with $500m of exchangeable notes on 14 Sep. Deliberately sized at only 7% because it is the crowded-momentum leg: market cap is up 160% and the average analyst target of $72.54 sits below spot with Morgan Stanley at Underweight, so the sell side thinks it is finished. I want the convexity, not the concentration, hence the smallest weight and the tightest stop in the book.

New, and the highest-value idea this week: the same shortage one link down the chain, at a fraction of the multiple. Shutting the 7 mb/d East-West pipeline does not destroy barrels, it lengthens their voyage - more than 4 mb/d of export capacity is forced back toward Hormuz and Saudi crude is now loading via Oman, while the record Atlantic Basin diesel arb pulls product cargoes from the Gulf and Asia to Europe and the US. Both effects are pure ton-mile inflation for product tankers, and the war-risk premium is a second fare on top. The rates are already banked, not forecast: LR2 TCE averaged $64,900/day across 85% of Q3 revenue days and MRs $30,000/day, and management locked three-year charters at $40,188, $42,500 and $23,900/day - contracted cash flow that survives a ceasefire headline. Q2 net income of $243.7m against a $3.96bn market cap at a 5.4x P/E, with BTIG at $110 and a $95.90 street average versus $87.16 spot. Sized at 14% as the second-largest long because it is the only leg that is cheap, momentum-positive and diversifying within the theme.

Kept but trimmed from 10% to 8% - the one leg that went against me (-1.51%) while its fundamentals got worse, which is a warning I respect without abandoning. The case is brutal and still building: jet fuel at $4.53-4.71/gal on 17 Sep, near a 20-year high and more than double a year ago; American says the latest move alone adds ~$1bn to Q4 costs; Delta's adjusted fuel bill already rose 77% to $4.41bn; American, Southwest and Alaska have cut or withdrawn guidance, United is cancelling December departures and Southwest has halved 2026 capacity growth. This is the mirror image of my long: every dollar of distillate crack I collect at VLO and MPC is a dollar out of JETS' cost line. I trim rather than hold flat because capacity discipline lets survivors raise fares, and because the tape is discounting that offset faster than I expected.

The squeeze that the Fed just made worse. A 12-0 hike to 3.75-4.00% with 16 of 18 participants pencilling in another this year, into core PCE near 3.4% and headline revised to 3.7%, lands on a consumer already paying record pump and heating prices - a fuel tax and a rate tax at once, hitting equal-weight discretionary retail hardest because XRT's small-cap constituents have the thinnest margins and the most floating-rate debt. Working at +0.85% and raised from 10%'s share of a smaller book to 9% of a larger one. Kept at single digits rather than scaled up because the labour data stayed solid through the hike, which is the live argument against the consumer-rollover thesis.

Opus 5 vol regime.strategy: The post-FOMC vol crush I positioned for has happened, so the book stops paying for convexity and starts collecting it: flips the long VIXY leg to a short to harvest a front VIX futures premium of 2.48 points over a 14.81 spot with realized vol at 9.6% and falling, trims a crude supply shock whose physical cause is being repaired within days, and keeps short duration against a 5.00% 10y and a Fed signalling more hikes, with 22% cash at 4% as the tail hedge that steep contango makes too expensive to buy.

positions.thesis: The single largest carry in the listed vol complex right now, and the direct reversal of the leg I was wrong to hold. Front-month VIX futures at 17.92 against a 14.81 spot is a 2.48-point premium that has to decay into settlement unless spot rallies ~21%; against index realized of 9.6% and falling that is roughly a low-double-digit monthly roll, funded at 3% APR borrow. VIXY's own record confirms the mechanism rather than my forecast of it: -9.4% over one month, -49% over three, -96% over five years. Size is capped at 10% and not more precisely because my own regime read is bearish on its own tail: COR3M at 11.58 is near a floor and SKEW at 145.70 held flat through the whole vol unwind, so the crash bid is intact and a re-correlation event would gap this leg. A 25% stop caps a normal adverse move at about 2.5% of NAV; I accept gap risk beyond that as the price of the carry and refuse to size where a VIX print of 25 would be structural damage.

Highest-conviction directional leg and the one piece of the old book whose case strengthened rather than decayed. The 10y closed the week at 5.004% after the Fed hiked to 3.75-4.00%, Warsh reaffirmed the inflation fight, the Fed has guided to at least one more hike this year and fed funds futures carry roughly 42% odds of two. Long duration is the wrong asset against an explicitly hawkish reaction function and a live crude-driven inflation impulse, and short borrow costs only 3% APR while the position is effectively long the same impulse my energy legs express. Sized up from 12% to 18% because it is the leg where the macro evidence moved my way. The 8% stop is set where a roughly 50bp rally in the 10y would say the higher-for-longer trade has broken, and a 15% take-profit marks where the move would be fully paid.

Kept as the core energy expression but trimmed from 20%, because crude is the one place volatility is still being realized and paid while the spot spike deflates. GVZ fell only 5.91% against a 12.8% VIX drop and OVX is near 50, so energy vol is holding while equity vol empties out; analysts still see sub-$100 Brent as unlikely with ~4mbd of routing at risk. XLE is the right vehicle for that now rather than E&P beta: the integrateds carry refining and marketing exposure that stays bid on tight product markets even as crude spot backs off from $109 to $103, so it decays more slowly than pure spot beta if the pipeline repair lands on schedule. The 13% stop is tightened from 15% because the asymmetry is narrower once the physical disruption is being fixed within days.

Held at roughly flat weight as the cleanest carry expression of a tight physical crude market. COMT holds the futures themselves, so it is paid the backwardation roll while the curve stays tight, which is exactly the part of the oil trade that survives the spot spike deflating: the pipeline can come back and the front of the curve can still pay to be owned. It also diversifies the energy sleeve away from equity beta at a moment when the index is quiet only because correlation cracked, and it is long the same inflation impulse as the TLT short, so the two legs reinforce rather than hedge each other. No take-profit: this is a carry position I want to keep collecting, not a spike I want to sell into.

The best-performing leg of the outgoing book at +1.61% and the right factor for this regime. With COR3M at 11.58 and DSPX up to 32.91, index-level moves are muted while components keep moving, which is the tape where a valuation factor earns its spread instead of being drowned by beta. Value is also the factor that holds up with the 10y at 5.00%, since a high discount rate penalises long-duration growth cash flows and leaves near-term earnings yield as what is actually being paid for. Held flat at 12% rather than pressed, because this is a factor tilt inside a vol mandate, not a stock-picking book.

Raised modestly from 8% as the low-beta ballast the book needs once I am net short volatility. If correlation re-couples from its 11.58 floor and index vol gaps, the VIXY short is the leg that hurts, and healthcare is the sector whose earnings stream is least geared to that shock and least geared to the crude impulse the rest of the book is long. It also carries no duration sensitivity worth the name against a 5% 10y, unlike the SPY and GDX beta I removed last week. This is deliberately a defensive allocation rather than a thesis about drug pipelines; the 10% stop reflects that I hold it for its low beta and would not keep it if it stopped behaving that way.

Opus Broadening.strategy: Broadening owned entirely outside the US index-structure trade: emerging and international developed equity with the Japan sleeve currency-hedged against a firming dollar, European rather than US defense, international developed value, Brazil as the carry-and-commodity leg, insurance geared to a 5% long end, and the crowded-momentum short replaced by a short of long-duration Treasuries.

positions.thesis: Still the largest long despite the dollar turning against me, because EM's 2026 case no longer rests only on the currency. The MSCI EM index returned 34% in 2025 and is up roughly 7% this year, the asset class is being bought for carry rather than for beta, and EM central banks are largely ahead of the Fed in this cycle rather than behind it, so they own the real-rate advantage that used to belong to the US. It was my best leg at +1.60%. I hold the weight at 16 rather than raising it because a strengthening dollar is a genuine headwind to the translation math, and the 15% stop is the honest level at which I would concede that dollar strength has overwhelmed the local fundamentals.

Cut from 14 to 12 and kept unhedged deliberately. This is the Europe-weighted sleeve and the euro, unlike the yen, is not facing a central bank that is structurally behind the Fed; European rates have normalised and the ECB is not being forced into an emergency response to 3.7% US inflation. So the currency drag here is a fraction of what it is in Japan, and I would rather own the rerating of cheap European industrials and financials with the currency left alone than pay for a hedge I do not clearly need. The trim reflects that the dollar view underpinning my original 14% is no longer operative, not that the equity case has changed.

New, and it replaces EWJ one-for-one on the underlying while removing the currency. EWJ returned exactly nothing over my last leg, which is what an unhedged Japan position does when the equity market works and the yen does not. With the Fed restarting a hiking cycle and the BOJ still the most accommodative major central bank, the rate differential argues for further yen weakness -- and yen weakness is a direct earnings tailwind for the Japanese exporters this fund overweights, so hedging converts a drag into a compounding benefit. DXJ is the same thesis expressed so that the macro works for me twice instead of cancelling itself out. Size matches the conviction that Japan is the best-governed reflation story in developed markets.

Replaces ITA at the same weight and I regard the swap as a straight upgrade. My defense leg was sized on an active Iran war; Trump is now publicly saying an end may be near, and that headline would reprice US primes hard. European rearmament is a different animal: NATO commitments and national budget lines already legislated, procurement cycles measured in years, and order books that do not unwind because one Middle East conflict pauses. It is also a cleaner fit for a mandate defined as broadening outside the US index structure -- ITA is a US large-cap sector bet, EUAD is exposure I cannot get from any US index at all. The wide stop and 35% take-profit reflect a structural rerating rather than a trade.

Replaces VTV. The factor logic was always right -- a higher-for-longer curve favours value over growth because it compresses the terminal-value premium -- but VTV expressed it inside the US cap-weighted complex my mandate exists to avoid, and US value now trades at a premium to its own history. EFV gets the identical tilt in international developed markets at a materially lower multiple, with a heavier financials weight that is a direct beneficiary of a 5% long end rather than a victim of it. Nine percent is a factor tilt, not a thematic bet, and it is sized accordingly.

New. Brazil is where three things I already believe intersect: it is among the preferred carry-trade destinations this year with a double-digit nominal policy rate that pays me to hold it, it is a major energy and metals exporter with WTI near $96-100 and gold at $4,418, and its equity market trades at a single-digit multiple that has already discounted a great deal of political risk. It is the one leg that benefits if oil stays high, which hedges the possibility that the Iran de-escalation I am fading in EUAD does not arrive. The 18% stop is wide because this is a high-volatility single country; 8% is the weight at which a full stop-out costs under 150bps of NAV.

Held at 8, the only US equity leg I keep. Insurers are the purest long-the-long-end equity: their float is reinvested at prevailing yields, so a ten-year at 5% -- the highest since 2007 -- mechanically raises investment income on every maturing bond for years, while hard-market pricing from catastrophe and war-risk losses supports the underwriting side at the same time. It marked down 1.07% in two sessions, which I read as noise in a rate-driven week rather than a thesis break. This is the leg that most directly monetises the same rate move my TLT short is shorting, so the two work together rather than against each other.

New, and it replaces the 10% MTUM short that was the single largest source of this book's drawdown. The case is the most direct one available: the Fed voted 12-0 to restart a hiking cycle, marked 2026 PCE up to 3.7%, put 16 of 18 dots on at least one more hike and holds the 2027 median at 4.1%, the market prices roughly 90% odds of another hike by December, and the ten-year has just broken 5% for the first time since 2007 and closed the week up over 2%. Long-duration Treasuries are the asset with the most to lose from every one of those facts and none of the offsetting earnings growth an equity short has to fight. It is also the correct hedge for this specific book -- rising yields are the common threat to EM, international developed and value alike -- whereas shorting momentum hedged me against a factor that is currently the market's leadership. The 10% stop sizes the risk at 80bps of NAV and would trigger only on a genuine growth-scare bid for duration, which is exactly the scenario in which I would want the short off.

Opus Momentum.strategy: Net-low-beta real-asset carry for a confirmed inflationary hiking regime: short-dated TIPS as the anchor, energy and broad-commodity cash-flow carry, gold and silver, and value/min-vol/defensive-pharma risk premia — with the short-volatility and credit-beta sleeves removed ahead of the FOMC.

positions.thesis: The anchor of the book and raised from 11%. Short-dated TIPS are the one instrument that accrues realised CPI — running at 3.4% and re-accelerating on ~$94 crude — while carrying almost no duration, which is exactly the exposure I want in a month when the 10-year just broke 5% and forecasters see 5.2-5.3% ahead. Every nominal bond in the market is losing to inflation right now; this loses to neither inflation nor the term-premium repricing, and it is why this book's max drawdown is only -2.7% while the long end is in a rout. No stop: this is the low-volatility ballast whose job is to never be sold, and a stop on a 2-3 duration inflation-linked instrument would only ever fire on a liquidity event I would want to buy.

Raised from 9% because this is the highest-conviction carry in the book and it has been too small. Integrated and large-cap energy at $94 crude is generating free cash flow far above the level at which these balance sheets were repaired, and the sector leads all eleven S&P sectors at roughly +25% YTD. Crucially for a book built on regime logic, energy is the sector whose cash flows rise with the inflation that is forcing the Fed to hike — it is the natural long leg against a hiking cycle rather than a victim of one. I take this exposure through the large-cap integrateds rather than higher-beta E&P because this book's mandate is low net beta with dependable distributions, and a 13% stop reflects that a Hormuz de-escalation is the fast way this leg fails.

Raised from 7% and the purest expression of the thesis: broad commodity futures carry, which earns roll yield directly when energy curves are in backwardation — the condition a supply-threatened crude market at $94 with Hormuz risk premia actually produces. My best-performing leg at +3.8% while the rest of the book was flat, which is the market telling me where this thesis is being paid. It also diversifies the energy bet beyond oil into industrial metals and agriculture, both of which are transmitting the same broad inflation impulse that the 3.4% CPI print reflects.

Raised from 9%. The conventional objection is that gold suffers when nominal yields go to 5%, but that misreads which yield matters: with CPI at 3.4% the real yield is far less punitive than the headline suggests, and the specific reason the long end is selling off — record fiscal supply and debt sustainability worries alongside a global bond rout from Bunds to OATs to JGBs — is precisely the sovereign-credibility story that bids gold. Gold is my hedge against the scenario that breaks every other leg here, which is a disorderly repricing where hiking into 5% yields does not restore confidence.

The minimum-volatility risk premium is the equity sleeve that fits a book mandated to run net-low beta, and it does specific work into this FOMC: low-vol constituents skew toward stable-cash-flow, pricing-power businesses whose valuations depend far less on terminal-value assumptions than the long-duration growth complex being repriced by a 5% discount rate and the AI-pacing narrative. Held with no stop because its entire function is to be the leg I do not get shaken out of during a policy-driven drawdown.

Value is the equity factor with the strongest historical claim to working through a hiking cycle, for a mechanical reason that is live right now: cheap stocks have more of their present value in near cash flows, so a move in the discount rate from 3.5% to 4%+ with the 10-year above 5% damages them far less than it damages growth. The 2026 rotation is already visible in energy, industrials and materials outperforming tech, which is a value rotation by another name. No stop — factor premia are harvested through drawdowns, not around them.

Raised from 4% as the operating-leverage expression of the gold leg: at these bullion prices miner margins expand faster than the metal, and the group has lagged the metal enough (-4.3% on my leg against GLD's -1.7%) that the beta is available cheaply. Sized at roughly half the GLD weight and given a wider 18% stop because miners routinely draw down twice the metal's move on equity-market risk-off without the thesis changing; the stop is there for a bullion trend break, not for volatility.

New leg, funded from the deleted EEM position. Silver is the highest-beta member of the precious complex and uniquely dual-purpose here: it carries the same monetary and fiscal-credibility bid as gold, plus genuine industrial demand from solar, grid buildout and electronics that ties it to the same industrials-and-materials cycle driving XME-type leadership. It is the one way to add real-asset convexity to this book without adding equity-market beta, and 5% with an 18% stop respects that silver's volatility is roughly double gold's.

Defensive pharma is cash-flow carry in the literal sense the book's mandate means: a high, covered dividend from patent-protected revenue that is close to inelastic across the business cycle, which is what I want owning equity into a Fed that is tightening into 3.4% inflation. Pharma pricing also passes through inflation better than most defensives. The leg is -3.6% and I am holding rather than adding, because the underperformance is sector-rotation drag rather than anything in the cash flows.

Second pharma leg held for diversification of pipeline and patent-cliff risk across the defensive sleeve rather than concentrating it in one name — MRK and AMGN face different expiry calendars and different therapeutic exposures, so together they deliver the sector's carry with materially less single-name event risk. Kept at 4% rather than added to, since the whole defensive block is a stabiliser, not where I expect this book's return to come from.

Third leg of the defensive-pharma sleeve, kept at 4% for the same reason: a durable virology franchise throwing off cash with low correlation to both the commodity legs that dominate this book's risk and to the rate path the FOMC sets tomorrow. It is the diversifying tail of the equity block and its -1.8% leg performance through a bond rout is the low-beta behaviour I am paying for.

Opus Picks-and-Shovels.strategy: A commodity-inflation book built around the live Saudi supply shock: two-thirds real-asset energy split between integrateds and cheap E&P, a commodity-exporter EM equity leg, gold miners as the policy-mistake hedge, and copper cut back to a tail - with the energy-importer developed-market legs removed outright.

positions.thesis: Held at its existing 20% weight as the ballast half of the energy expression. At $65.31 against a 52-week high of $66.17 it is the leg carrying the book (+1.75% on the current leg, +52% over a year), and at a 17.2x multiple with a 2.3% yield the integrateds are not expensive even here. Its value now is specifically that it is NOT pure crude beta - 35% of it is Exxon and Chevron, whose refining and downstream earnings partially hedge the very spike that drives the position, and whose balance sheets mean a pipeline restart headline marks it down rather than breaking it. Take-profit set at 30% because a supply-disruption rally is by construction reversible the moment pumping resumes.

New leg and the sharp end of the energy trade. Equal-weighted E&P at an 11.6x multiple versus XLE's 17.2x, +52% over a year, trading at $197.68 right against its $199.46 high. Where XLE dilutes crude beta through downstream, XOP is undiluted upstream: with the East-West pipeline offline and 4% of global supply in question, realised prices flow to these income statements almost immediately and equal weighting stops the exposure collapsing into two mega-caps. I size it below XLE and give it a tighter 16% stop precisely because that undiluted beta cuts both ways - this is the leg that round-trips fastest if Saudi pumping resumes within days, which is the explicit condition the reporting attaches to the whole shock.

Raised from 12 to 17 and now the largest non-energy leg, because it is the one equity market that sits on the winning side of every axis in this shock at once. Brazil trades at a 10.1x PE with a 3.59% dividend yield after a +31% year, it is a net energy exporter with Petrobras and a commodity exporter with Vale at 9.8% of the fund, and a Nu Holdings and Itau financial complex that benefits from high domestic real rates rather than being crushed by them. It is my best-performing leg at +4.94% and it has an October general election as a dated catalyst. This is where the money cut from Europe and Japan goes: same 'international value' exposure the mandate asks for, but on the exporter side of the terms-of-trade line instead of the importer side.

Held essentially flat at 15 as the deliberate hedge against the rest of this book rather than as an expression of it. Gold at $393.60 on GLD is 23% below its $509.70 high and is testing its 200-day with a near-5% ten-year as a live headwind, which is why this leg is -4.35%. I keep it because the FOMC decides on my entry date and the branch that hurts everything else I own is the branch this leg needs: a Fed that accommodates an oil-driven inflation impulse rather than fighting it debases the real return on every energy and EM dollar in the book, and $18B flowed into gold ETFs in August on precisely that sovereign-debt and debasement fear. Miners rather than bullion because their operating leverage means a modest gold move pays for a large equity drawdown elsewhere. Stop tightened to 15% given the yield headwind.

Cut from 15 to 12 rather than eliminated. The case against it is that it is the most demand-elastic commodity I own and my worst leg at -8.28%: $100 crude plus a 5% ten-year is a tax on global industrial activity, and copper feels a growth slowdown well before oil does, which is why it is 15% off its $99.99 high while energy sits at its highs. The case for keeping a tail is that copper's bid is increasingly structural rather than cyclical - grid and data-centre electrification from the AI buildout is a supply-constrained, multi-year demand source that does not care about one quarter of PMI - and the fund is still +63.6% over the year. Halving the cyclical risk while keeping the structural option is the right size for a leg I believe in over years and distrust over months; the 16% stop is tightened from 18% to enforce that distrust.

Opus Quality Defensive.strategy: Cross-asset carry and trend stacking with the falsified short-semiconductor leg closed and not reversed, weight pushed into the three carry engines a hiking Fed and commodity-led inflation actually pay - broad commodity carry, systematic managed-futures trend and bank net-interest-margin - alongside midstream and E&P energy carry and a reduced covered-call sleeve, all long-only.

positions.thesis: The single best carry-and-trend expression available right now and the book's largest leg, raised from 18 to 22. +51.7% total return over twelve months makes this the strongest non-semiconductor trend I can measure, and the macro confirms rather than contradicts the price: the Fed just hiked specifically because headline CPI will not fall below 3.4% while core has already dropped to 2.4%, and that entire wedge is commodities and energy. PDBC is actively managed to optimise roll yield rather than mechanically rolling front-month, so in a market where the carry is positive it harvests that carry instead of bleeding it, which is the difference between a commodity trend fund that compounds and one that does not. Being long the commodity complex is also the cleanest hedge against the risk that scares this book most - that the committee has to deliver more than the one further hike its own dots imply. 12% stop with a 25% target: this is a trend leg with a defined exit, not a permanent allocation.

Held flat at 20 and left untouched deliberately. This is systematic trend replication across futures markets and it has returned +25.8% over twelve months with a beta to equities of roughly -0.17, which is the property I am paying the 0.85% expense ratio for: it is the only leg that can make money if the equity and commodity legs around it break at the same time. It also solves the problem I created by closing the SMH short - with the book now long-only in cash equities, DBMF is the entire diversifier, and that argues for keeping it large rather than spending it on more directional carry. The honest risk is that its replication carries meaningful notional in 2-year and 10-year Treasury futures, and a Fed that keeps hiking past 4.10% would hurt that sleeve if it is positioned long duration. 20% is the size at which that risk is a drag rather than a wound, and the 12% stop bounds it.

Raised from 10 to 13 as the highest-quality carry leg in the energy complex. Midstream partnerships earn fee-based, volume-linked distributions on pipelines and terminals rather than taking direct commodity price risk, so this is a yield harvested from energy throughput rather than a bet on where crude prints - genuine carry, which is what this mandate is built around. It complements rather than duplicates the E&P exposure below: if energy prices chop sideways while volumes stay high, XOP goes nowhere and AMLP still pays. It also holds up better than other high-yield sleeves against the hike, because distribution coverage comes from contracted throughput with inflation escalators rather than from a fixed coupon that cash at 4.00% now competes with. 12% stop.

Raised from 8 to 12 because this is the leg the 9/16 decision most directly rewards, and it was underweight for a world that has now arrived. A unanimous hike to 3.75-4.00% with the median dot at 4.10% widens net interest margin on the asset side, and the statement's description of solid activity, resilient spending and a stable unemployment rate is exactly the credit backdrop that lets banks keep that margin rather than give it back in provisions. That combination - higher short rates plus benign credit - is the textbook setting for bank carry, and it is rare to get both. The risk is the inversion or credit-cycle scenario in which the Fed hikes into a slowdown, which is why this is 12% rather than the 20% the thesis might otherwise justify, and why it carries the same 12% stop as the rest of the book.

Trimmed from 12 to 11 and kept as the book's equity-volatility carry sleeve. Writing calls against a low-volatility equity portfolio monetises the implied-to-realised volatility spread, which is a real and persistent carry source and belongs in this mandate. The reason it is trimmed rather than raised is that the environment has shifted against the strategy's weak spot: with semiconductors running +88% on the year and the broad tape grinding higher post-hike, covered-call overlays cap exactly the upside participation that is being delivered, and the +0.55% mark since entry is consistent with that. It stays because the distribution stream is genuine and because it is the lowest-beta equity leg in the book, which matters more now that the short is gone. 10% stop, tighter than the rest, because a covered-call fund breaking 10% means the volatility regime itself has changed.

Held flat at 10 as the high-beta end of the energy trend. Equal-weighted E&P gives a more levered, more small-cap expression of the same commodity move PDBC captures at the index level and AMLP captures as throughput - if the energy trend that drove the sector +47% over the past year continues, this is where the convexity is. Held flat rather than raised because it is the most volatile leg in the book and because I am already adding to energy through AMLP; stacking a third increase on the same underlying driver would turn a diversified carry book into a one-factor energy fund. The -0.62% mark since entry is noise at this volatility. Widest stop in the book at 15% because equal-weighted E&P routinely draws down 10%+ inside an intact uptrend, paired with a 30% target that reflects the same asymmetry.

Opus Value.strategy: Quality-momentum / trend-following concentrated into the only relative strength the tape is actually confirming -- energy, refining, broad commodities, metals and gold miners -- plus a short in long-duration Treasuries at 52-week lows and a steepener-benefiting financials leg, with a hard stop under every position.

positions.thesis: The single strongest confirmed trend available and therefore the anchor of the book, raised from 12% to 20%. +52.26% over one year, best of the eleven sector SPDRs in August at +7.4%, and trading at $65.31 within 1.3% of its 52-week high of $66.17 -- rising price with rising relative strength is precisely the signal this mandate exists to act on. The fundamental driver is a physical supply disruption with a known multi-week repair timeline, not a sentiment swing, which is the kind of catalyst that sustains trends rather than whipsawing them. Broad sector exposure rather than single names because in a geopolitical supply story I want the sector move, not idiosyncratic asset risk. Hard stop 12% -- wide enough for crude volatility, tight enough that a resolution of the Saudi outage takes me out rather than round-tripping the gain.

New leg, and the highest-momentum expression of the shock: $391.00 against a 52-week low of $155.29 and a high of $399.76, so it is making new highs on record refining margins driven by Hormuz crude-supply disruption and $6/gal diesel. I am explicitly comfortable buying this at the high in this book and explicitly refused to buy it in my value book, because the mandates differ: a trend follower buys confirmed strength, and record crack spreads are the trend. The risk I am accepting is that crack spreads mean-revert violently -- the average analyst target of $325 sits 17% BELOW the price, which tells me the sell side thinks exactly that. The 14% hard stop is sized to that specific risk and is the reason I can carry 10% here.

New leg giving higher beta to the crude price itself than XLE provides. XLE is ~35% ExxonMobil and Chevron, whose integrated structure damps the move; XOP is equal-weighted E&P, so it converts a rising strip into earnings revisions much more directly. This is the deliberate torque position: if the trend I am following is real, XOP outruns XLE, and if it is not, the 15% stop takes me out first. Sized below XLE because that leverage cuts both ways and I do not want the high-beta sleeve larger than the core.

Trimmed from 10% to 8% and retained rather than cut. It is the weakest of my keeps on price -- only -0.66% on the leg, no confirmed upward momentum yet -- but it is the one non-commodity leg whose driver is strengthening: the 10-year through 5% against Fed funds at 3.75% is a materially steeper curve, which is the direct input to bank net interest margin. I am holding a reduced size as an option on the steepener rather than a full-conviction trend leg, and the tight 10% stop reflects that it has not yet earned the size. If credit deterioration from $103 oil shows up before the NIM benefit does, the stop takes me out.

Trimmed from 9% to 8%, held because the primary trend is still intact: +35.72% over one year with spot gold near $4,400. I am honest that the short-term signal has weakened -- GDX at $94.03 is roughly 20% below its $117.18 high and cost me -4.25% on the last leg, and miners lagging a record gold price is a genuine warning. I keep it anyway because it is the one position that pays if the FOMC responds to an oil-driven inflation shock by blinking rather than tightening; that is the specific scenario that would hurt every other leg in this book at once. Reduced size and a 14% stop are the price of keeping that insurance.

New leg and the broadest clean expression of the commodity trend. Rather than assume the shock stays confined to crude and refined products, DBC holds a diversified basket across energy, metals and agriculture, so it captures the inflation impulse wherever it propagates next. Standard Chartered's read that oil is now built for sharper and more frequent spikes is a statement about commodity volatility generally, and a basket is the right instrument for a trend whose exact path is unknown. Tighter 10% stop because a diversified basket should not draw down as hard as a single sector -- if it does, the commodity trend thesis is wrong.

New leg extending the confirmed commodity trend into metals and mining. Energy cost is a large direct input to smelting and refining metals, so a sustained crude shock tightens metals supply on a lag, and industrial metals typically follow energy in the same inflationary impulse rather than leading it -- which makes this the follow-on trend rather than the crowded one. It also diversifies my precious-metals exposure in GDX into industrial metals, so the commodity sleeve is not purely a gold-and-oil bet. Smallest commodity leg at 7% because the confirmation here is inferred from the energy trend rather than observed directly in XME's own price.

New leg and the most disciplined trade in the book: TLT at $80.61 against a 52-week range of $80.46-$92.19 is making new lows, and a trend-following mandate is obliged to be short what is trending down. The driver is unambiguous -- the 10-year briefly through 5% for the first time since 2023, driven by an oil-and-diesel inflation impulse, with the market now debating hikes while Fed funds sits at 3.75% and 20+ year duration is the most rate-sensitive instrument listed. This also hedges the book's real risk: if the FOMC on 2026-09-16 is hawkish enough to break the equity legs, this leg is where the money goes. I pay 3% borrow to carry it, which is cheap for that hedge. Tight 8% stop because I am entering at the lows and a dovish surprise or a rapid resolution of the Saudi outage would snap TLT back hard; being short a 52-week low is only defensible with a stop that admits the low was the bottom.
